common_name: Pink Frost Hellebore (Gold Collection Marbled-Leaf Hybrid Hellebore)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in fall or early spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Pink Frost is a compact Gold Collection hybrid prized for silver-marbled, spiny-edged foliage and clusters of dusty-pink to plum-flushed white flowers that open in late winter and deepen in color with age.

directions: Set divisions or container plants into humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial shade, since this Helleborus niger x lividus hybrid resents both waterlogging and prolonged drought. Pink Frost stands out among hellebores for its silvery, marbled evergreen leaves veined in green, which remain attractive through the growing season and pair well with the nodding, rose-flushed white flowers produced on branching stems above the foliage in late winter. Being a patented Gold Collection selection, it is propagated by division or tissue culture rather than seed, and clumps benefit from occasional dividing every three to four years to maintain vigor. Remove tattered old foliage in late winter just before bloom to showcase the flowers.

common_name: Wintergold Hellebore (Gold Collection Golden-Flowered Hybrid Hellebore)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in fall or early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wintergold is a vigorous Gold Collection cross of Helleborus niger and H. argutifolius that combines spiny, leathery foliage with unusually soft golden-yellow flowers blushed pink as they age.

directions: Site in fertile, humus-rich soil with good drainage in partial shade, mulching lightly to conserve moisture and moderate soil temperature over winter. Wintergold inherits the coarse, spiny-toothed, dark evergreen foliage of Corsican hellebore parentage along with the earlier, more floriferous blooming habit of Christmas rose, producing abundant outward-facing flowers that open a soft primrose-yellow and age to dusky pink as the season progresses. This nigercors hybrid is notably vigorous and more heat-tolerant than pure Helleborus niger selections, making it a useful choice where straight Christmas rose struggles. As a patented clone it is increased by division rather than seed; established clumps can be lifted and split in early fall once flowering slows.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to a bit more sun than most hellebores tolerate; H. x sternii, a cross of H. argutifolius and H. lividus, is grown chiefly for its stiff, silver-marbled, purple-tinged evergreen foliage as much as for its pale green flowers flushed pink.

directions: Grow in gritty, well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH in partial shade; this hybrid tolerates more sun and dry spells than most hellebores, a trait inherited from its Mediterranean parent species. Helleborus x sternii forms a tidy, shrubby clump of leathery, spine-toothed leaves heavily veined and marbled in silver over blue-green, often flushed with purple-red along the margins and stems, giving strong foliage interest even without bloom. In late winter, branched clusters of cupped, pale jade-green flowers often tinged rose-pink appear above the foliage, echoing the purplish stem color. Because named selections do not come true from seed, propagate by division of the crown or by basal cuttings taken in spring.

common_name: Royal Heritage Hellebore (Royal Heritage Strain Lenten Rose)

planting.note: Set young transplants in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial to full shade; Royal Heritage is a long-established seed strain bred for outward-facing flowers and a wide color range from white through pink, rose, purple, and near-black.

directions: Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, working in compost at planting to mimic the leaf-litter conditions the species favors in the wild. Royal Heritage is a strain of Lenten rose developed over decades of selective breeding, prized for producing a higher proportion of outward-facing to upward-facing flowers than older seed strains, in a broad palette spanning white, cream, pink, rose, plum, and near-black, frequently with contrasting freckling or picotee edges. Because it is a seed strain rather than a single clone, individual seedlings vary somewhat in color and form, which many gardeners consider part of its charm. Cut back tattered old leaves in late winter before the flower stalks emerge, and allow self-sown seedlings to mature nearby if a naturalized drift is desired.

common_name: Southern Comfort Heuchera (Giant Peach-Amber Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Southern Comfort is a Heuchera villosa hybrid selected for oversized, ruffled amber-peach leaves and strong heat and humidity tolerance, making it dependable in warm-summer regions where thinner-leaved heucheras decline.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some afternoon shelter in hot climates, since the villosa parentage gives this cultivar unusual tolerance for heat and humidity compared to many coral bells. Southern Comfort produces an unusually large, mounding rosette of ruffled, maple-shaped leaves that emerge peachy-apricot and mature to a warm caramel-amber with rosy undersides, creating a bold textural accent well above the size of most heuchera cultivars. Airy sprays of small cream to pale pink flowers rise on wiry stems in early summer but are secondary to the foliage display. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, replanting the youngest rosettes at the original soil depth to avoid crown rot.

common_name: Plum Pudding Heuchera (Silver-Veined Purple Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Plum Pudding is a long-popular cultivar valued for deep purple, ruffled foliage overlaid with prominent silvery venation that shows best with a few hours of morning sun.

directions: Set divisions into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving a few hours of gentle morning sun where possible to intensify the leaf color without scorching. Plum Pudding forms a tight mound of ruffled, rounded leaves in a rich aubergine-purple with a network of raised silver veins and wine-red undersides, holding its color well into autumn. It sends up thin, wiry flower stalks with small greenish-white bells in early summer, which many gardeners shear off to keep the focus on foliage. This older, well-tested cultivar is reliably vigorous and clumping rather than spreading, and benefits from division every few years once the central crown begins to heave out of the soil.

common_name: Electric Lime Heuchera (Chartreuse Ruffled Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Electric Lime is a bright chartreuse-foliaged coral bells selection that lights up shaded borders and combines especially well with dark-leaved companions.

directions: Grow in evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, protecting from hot midday sun which can bleach the vivid foliage color. Electric Lime forms a dense, ruffled mound of glossy, lime-to-chartreuse leaves with fine red venation radiating from the center, providing strong color contrast against purple-leaved heucheras, dark hostas, or black mondo grass. Slender flower spikes bearing small white to pale pink bells appear in early summer above the foliage, attracting hummingbirds and small pollinators. Like most Heuchera cultivars it resents heavy, wet clay, so amend planting sites with compost or grit, and divide clumps every three to four years to maintain vigorous new growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade; Solar Eclipse is a Heucherella prized for deeply lobed, near-black leaves rimmed in bright chartreuse-green, spreading gradually by short stolons to form a groundcover patch.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist but well-drained soil in partial shade, since Heucherella hybrids generally need more consistent moisture than pure Heuchera selections. Solar Eclipse produces deeply cut, star-shaped leaves that emerge dark purple-black in the center fading to a bright green rim, a dramatic combination that intensifies in cooler weather. Unlike clumping heucheras, this Heuchera x Tiarella hybrid spreads slowly by short stolons, eventually knitting together into a dense groundcover patch useful for edging shaded beds. Loose sprays of small white flowers appear in late spring; shear spent stalks after bloom and divide the spreading mat every few years to control its size or propagate new plants.
